analogy.p: Imagine filming a runner with a flip-book camera. The **sample rate** is how many photos you take each second: 4 photos per second leave big jumps between pictures, but 60 per second show every smooth movement. The **bit depth** is how finely you measure the runner's position in each photo: if you only mark 'left', 'middle' or 'right' (2 bits = 4 positions) you lose precision, but if you measure to the nearest millimetre (many bits) you capture it accurately. The **duration** is how long you film. More photos, finer measurements and a longer film all need a thicker album, which is the larger file size. The analogy breaks down because photos show the whole scene while a sound sample is just a single number, the wave's height at that instant, and a computer rebuilds the sound by joining those numbers, not by flicking through pictures.

bullets: **Analogue** = continuous signal that can take any value; **digital** = a limited set of separate values stored as binary.
Computers use binary because their circuits only have two reliable states (on/off), so everything stored, including sound, must be a pattern of 1s and 0s.
The J277 specification asks you to know how sound is **sampled and stored in digital form**, and how **sample rate, duration and bit depth** affect the size and quality of a sound file.
Stored digital sound can be copied again and again with no loss and can be edited, compressed and streamed, which is why music and speech are stored digitally.
Digitising always involves **approximation**: the digital version is a close copy of the analogue sound, never a perfect one.
The device that converts the wave into binary is an **analogue to digital converter (ADC)**; the device that turns the binary back into sound is a **digital to analogue converter (DAC)**.
core.h: Analogue sound and why it has to be converted
core.p: Sound is a **vibration that travels through the air as a wave**. A real sound wave is **analogue**: it is continuous, which means its pressure (and so the loudness, or **amplitude**) can take any value at every instant, with infinitely many tiny steps between any two moments. A computer can only store **discrete** (separate) values made of **binary** (1s and 0s). So a sound has to be converted from a smooth, continuous wave into a long list of binary numbers before it can be stored, edited, copied or sent over a network. That conversion is called **digitising** the sound, and the main idea behind it is **sampling**.

bullets: A **sample** is one measurement of the wave's amplitude at one instant.
Samples are taken at **equal time intervals**, so only the amplitude values need to be stored, in order.

Each sample amplitude is rounded to the nearest value that can be stored using the available number of bits; this rounding is called **quantisation** (a useful word, but the spec phrase is simply 'bit depth').
Between two samples the computer has no information at all about what the wave did, so it joins the points to estimate the shape.
The time gap between samples is **1 divided by the sample rate**: at 44,100 Hz the gap is 1 / 44,100 = about 0.0000227 s (22.7 microseconds).
Figure 1 shows an analogue wave with the sample points marked as dots on it; each dot becomes one binary number.
More samples per second means the dots are closer together and the rebuilt wave follows the original more faithfully.
core.p: **Sampling** means measuring the **amplitude** (height) of the sound wave at **regular, fixed intervals of time**. Each individual measurement is called a **sample**. Think of taking the wave's temperature, so to speak, many times every second: each reading is written down as a number. Because the samples are taken at equal time gaps, the computer does not need to store the time of every sample, only the list of values in order. When the samples are played back in the same order at the same speed, the computer can rebuild a wave that is very close to the original.

bullets: Sample rate = samples per second, measured in **Hz** (hertz).
1 kHz = 1,000 Hz, so 8 kHz = 8,000 Hz and 44.1 kHz = 44,100 Hz.
**Higher sample rate = higher quality (closer to the original) but a larger file.**
**Lower sample rate = lower quality (less detailed, can sound dull or 'muffled') but a smaller file.**
The sample rate is fixed for the whole recording, so the gaps between samples are all equal.
Typical values: telephone about 8,000 Hz; CD music 44,100 Hz; a lot of video and studio audio 48,000 Hz.

Extension (not needed for J277 calculations): to capture a frequency properly you need to sample at **more than twice** that frequency. Humans hear up to about 20,000 Hz, so a rate above 40,000 Hz, such as 44,100 Hz, covers the range of human hearing.
core.p: The **sample rate** is the **number of samples taken every second**. It is measured in **hertz (Hz)**, where 1 Hz means one sample per second. Because real sample rates are large they are usually written in **kilohertz (kHz)**: 1 kHz = 1,000 Hz, so 44.1 kHz = 44,100 Hz. A higher sample rate captures the wave in more detail, because the measurements are closer together in time, so fast changes in the sound are less likely to be missed. The price is that there are more numbers to store for every second of sound.

bullets: Bit depth = number of bits per sample.
Number of possible levels = **2^bit depth**: 1 bit gives 2 levels, 2 bits give 4, 4 bits give 16, 8 bits give 256, 16 bits give 65,536, 24 bits give 16,777,216.
**Higher bit depth = more levels = each sample is closer to the true amplitude = better quality, but every sample takes more bits so the file is larger.**
**Lower bit depth = fewer levels = bigger rounding errors, heard as a rough or hissy sound, but a smaller file.**
A bit depth of 16 is used for CDs; 8 is used for low quality voice recordings; 24 is used in professional recording.
Figure 2 shows the same wave stored with 2 bits (4 levels, a coarse staircase) and 4 bits (16 levels, a much closer fit).
Do not mix this up with colour depth for images: the idea is the same (bits per item) but sound uses bits per **sample**, images use bits per **pixel**.
core.p: The **bit depth** (also called the sample resolution) is the **number of bits used to store each sample**. It controls how many different amplitude values can be stored. With **n** bits there are **2 to the power n** different binary patterns, so there are 2^n possible amplitude levels. A higher bit depth lets each sample be recorded more precisely, because the amplitude is rounded to a much closer level. This is a different idea from sample rate: sample rate is about **when** (how often) the wave is measured, bit depth is about **how accurately** each measurement is recorded.

bullets: Duration is measured in **seconds** in the file-size formula; convert minutes to seconds first (x 60).
Number of samples = sample rate x duration.
Doubling the duration doubles the file size (they are **directly proportional**).
**Duration affects file size but not quality.**
A 3 minute track is 3 x 60 = 180 seconds; a 90 s clip is 90 seconds; 2 minutes 30 seconds is 150 seconds.
A common error is to leave the duration in minutes, which gives an answer that is 60 times too small.
core.p: The **duration** is the **length of the recording in seconds**. Because the computer takes the same number of samples every second, the total number of samples is simply the sample rate multiplied by the duration. So a recording that lasts twice as long contains twice as many samples and has a file that is twice as big, if nothing else is changed. Duration does not change the quality of the sound at all; it only changes how much data there is. This makes it different from sample rate and bit depth, which change both quality and size.

bullets: Step 1: sound waves reach the **microphone**.
Step 2: the microphone makes an **analogue electrical signal** that varies in the same pattern as the wave.
Step 3: the **ADC** measures the signal's amplitude at regular intervals (the sample rate).
Step 4: each measurement is converted to a **binary number** with the chosen bit depth.
Step 5: the binary numbers are saved in order in a **file** (and may be compressed).
The sample rate and bit depth are chosen **before** recording; they cannot be improved afterwards because the detail was never captured.
Recording at a higher quality than you need wastes storage; recording at a lower one loses detail permanently.
core.h: Recording sound step by step (analogue to digital)
core.p: When you record on a phone or computer, the sound goes through a chain of stages. The **microphone** converts the pressure variations of the sound wave into a varying electrical signal, which is still analogue. The **analogue to digital converter (ADC)** then **samples** that signal at the chosen sample rate and rounds each sample to a level that fits within the bit depth, producing one binary number per sample. Finally the stream of binary numbers is **stored** in a sound file, usually with a little extra data such as the sample rate and bit depth so a player knows how to read it. Figure 4 shows the whole chain.

bullets: The DAC changes **binary values back into an analogue signal**.
The amplifier increases the strength (power) of the signal; the speaker converts it into a sound wave.
The rebuilt wave is an **approximation** of the original, since the detail between samples and the rounding of values is lost.
Higher sample rate and higher bit depth make the rebuilt wave closer to the original.
Playing back at a different rate from the recording rate changes the pitch and speed (for example, too fast makes a voice sound high and quick).
Figure 4 shows the playback chain: stored file, DAC, amplifier, speaker.
core.p: To play a sound file the process is run in reverse. The player reads the binary samples in order at the correct sample rate. The **digital to analogue converter (DAC)** turns each binary number back into an electrical voltage, and the voltages are smoothed into a continuous signal that follows the sampled shape. An amplifier makes the signal strong enough to move the cone of a **speaker**, which pushes the air to create sound waves you can hear. Because the DAC must output samples at the same rate that they were recorded, playing a file at the wrong sample rate changes the speed and pitch of the sound.

bullets: **Higher sample rate: more samples per second, a more accurate (closer) copy of the original wave, higher quality.**
**Lower sample rate: fewer samples per second, more of the original detail is missed, lower quality.**
The cost of a higher rate is a **bigger file** and more storage and bandwidth needed.
Speech needs a lower sample rate than music because speech has fewer high frequencies, which is why the telephone can use about 8,000 Hz.
Mark scheme language: 'more samples are taken per second, so the sound is closer to the original / more accurate'.
Do not say that a higher sample rate makes the sound 'louder'; loudness is the amplitude, not the sample rate.
Do not say that it makes the sound 'higher pitched': pitch is the frequency of the sound, not how often it is sampled.
core.p: A higher sample rate gives more points per second to describe the wave, so the rebuilt wave has less distance between points where the computer has to guess. With a very low sample rate, rapid changes in the wave fall in the gaps between samples and are lost, so the sound loses its high pitched detail and can sound dull, muffled or distorted. Figure 3 compares a wave sampled only 4 times per cycle with the same wave sampled 16 times per cycle: the second set of points reproduces the curve much more smoothly. Always link your statement to the **closeness of the digital recording to the original sound**.

bullets: **Higher bit depth: more possible levels, each sample is more precise, higher quality, larger file.**
**Lower bit depth: fewer levels, bigger rounding errors, lower quality, smaller file.**
Levels = 2^bits: going from 8 bits (256 levels) to 16 bits (65,536 levels) is 256 times as many levels, but only twice the data per sample.
Increasing bit depth by 1 bit doubles the number of levels.
Bit depth does not change the speed of playback or the pitch.
A mark scheme phrase: 'more bits per sample means a more accurate / precise value is stored for each sample'.
core.p: A higher bit depth gives more possible amplitude values, so each sample can be stored closer to the real value of the wave at that moment. With a low bit depth, the real amplitude must be rounded to one of only a few levels and the rounding errors are large, which is heard as a rough, crackly or noisy sound. This is easy to see in Figure 2: the 2-bit staircase has only four heights to choose from, so it is far from the dashed original, but the 4-bit staircase with 16 heights follows the wave closely. Bit depth also controls the range between the quietest and loudest sounds that can be stored accurately.

bullets: **File size (bits) = sample rate (Hz) x bit depth x duration (seconds).**
Convert bits to bytes by **dividing by 8** (1 byte = 8 bits).
Convert bytes to kilobytes by dividing by 1,000, megabytes by dividing by 1,000,000, and so on (OCR uses 1,000 for each step in J277).
Convert **minutes to seconds** and **kHz to Hz** first.
The result ignores metadata and any compression; unless the question says so, give the uncompressed size.
If the question says the sound is stereo with two channels you would multiply by 2; J277 questions normally use a single channel unless told otherwise.
Write the unit with the answer: bits, bytes, kB or MB as asked.
core.p: The file size of an uncompressed sound recording is found by multiplying three things together: the sample rate, the bit depth and the duration. This gives the total number of **bits**, and you then convert to bytes and larger units. The formula is **file size (bits) = sample rate (Hz) x bit depth (bits) x duration (s)**. Each part makes sense: sample rate x duration = total number of samples, and each sample takes bit-depth bits. Always show every step in the exam because marks are awarded for the method, and always check that your units are right.

bullets: Sample rate (Hz) = file size (bits) / (bit depth x duration).
Bit depth = file size (bits) / (sample rate x duration).
Duration (s) = file size (bits) / (sample rate x bit depth).
Start by converting: bytes x 8 = bits; kB x 1,000 = bytes.
Example: a 5 s recording at 16-bit is 400,000 bytes = 3,200,000 bits, so sample rate = 3,200,000 / (16 x 5) = 40,000 Hz.
Check: 40,000 x 16 x 5 = 3,200,000 bits = 400,000 bytes, which matches.
Use brackets or do the multiplication in the denominator first, otherwise you may divide wrongly.
core.p: Exam questions can give you the file size and ask for a missing value, such as the duration or sample rate. Because the formula is a simple multiplication, you rearrange it by dividing by the other two values. Always convert the file size into **bits** first if the other quantities use bits and seconds, since the formula gives bits. Check the answer by putting it back into the original formula, which should return the file size you started with.

bullets: **Telephone / voice call:** about 8,000 Hz and 8 bits: small data, speech remains understandable but sounds thin.
**CD quality music:** 44,100 Hz and 16 bits: high quality for listening.
**Studio recording:** 48,000 Hz or higher and 24 bits: very high quality, big files.
One minute at 44,100 Hz and 16 bits (one channel) is 44,100 x 16 x 60 = 42,336,000 bits = 5,292,000 bytes, about 5.3 MB.
The same minute at 8,000 Hz and 8 bits is 8,000 x 8 x 60 = 3,840,000 bits = 480,000 bytes = 480 kB, about 11 times smaller.
Large sound files can be reduced with **compression** (lossy or lossless), which is a separate topic in the specification.
In an exam, a good answer states the benefit AND the cost: 'higher quality but larger file size'.
core.h: Comparing sound settings: trade-offs and real examples
core.p: Choosing sample rate and bit depth is always a **trade-off between quality and file size**. High settings give a faithful recording but need a lot of storage space and take longer to download or stream. Low settings save space and bandwidth but lose detail. The right choice depends on the use: a voice call only needs to be understandable, so a low sample rate and bit depth is enough, while a music master recording needs high values so it can be edited and processed without losing quality.

bullets: Straight line through the origin means **direct proportion**: zero sample rate means zero data.
The **gradient** of the graph is the number of bytes per kHz (here 20 kB for each kHz, because 1,000 samples x 16 bits x 10 s / 8 = 20,000 bytes).
When a table gives sample rates and file sizes, check by dividing: file size / sample rate should be constant if bit depth and duration are the same.
Changing the sample rate from 8 kHz to 44.1 kHz multiplies file size by 44.1 / 8 = about 5.5.
If a question gives a graph of quality against file size, the typical pattern is that quality improves more and more slowly while the file size keeps growing (diminishing returns).
State both axes and units when you describe a graph.
core.h: Reading graphs and tables about sound
core.p: Because file size depends on the three values multiplied together, the relationships are simple. If you double the sample rate, the file size doubles; if you double the bit depth, it doubles; if you double the duration, it doubles. Plotting file size against any one of these (keeping the others fixed) gives a **straight line through the origin**, which is called a **directly proportional** relationship. Figure 5 shows this for sample rate: a 10 second, 16-bit recording is 160 kB at 8 kHz, 441 kB at 22.05 kHz and 882 kB at 44.1 kHz.

bullets: **Binary:** each sample is stored as a binary number.
**Units:** bits, bytes, kB, MB, GB with factors of 8 and 1,000.
**Images:** sound uses sample rate and bit depth; images use resolution and colour depth. Both multiply quantities together to get file size.
**Compression:** lossy compression removes some detail to cut file size; lossless keeps all the data and can be rebuilt exactly.
**Networks:** bigger files take longer to transmit and use more bandwidth, so streaming services often lower the bitrate on slow connections.
**Storage:** high-quality sound needs more secondary storage space.
**Ethics/environment:** large files use more energy to store and transfer.
core.p: Sound representation links to many other parts of the J277 course, and examiners like answers that show the connections. It applies the ideas of **binary**, **units of data storage** and **converting between units**, and the sound file size formula is the audio version of the image file size formula (pixels x colour depth). It links to **compression**, because sound files are often compressed using lossy (for example MP3) or lossless methods, and to **networks and the internet**, since larger sound files need more bandwidth to stream and longer to download. It also links to **hardware**, as microphones, speakers and sound cards contain the ADC and DAC.

exam: **State/Give (1 mark):** a short fact such as 'sample rate is the number of samples taken per second' or 'bit depth is the number of bits used to store each sample'. No explanation needed.
**Identify (1 mark):** pick the right word from a list; learn the definitions of sample rate, bit depth and duration exactly.

**Describe how sound is stored digitally (2 to 3 marks):** the sound wave is sampled at regular intervals; the amplitude at each point is measured; each measurement is stored as a binary number; the numbers are stored in order.

**Explain the effect of increasing the sample rate (2 marks):** more samples are taken per second so the recording is closer to / a more accurate copy of the original sound (1); but the file size is larger (1).
**Explain the effect of increasing bit depth (2 marks):** each sample is stored with more bits so can be more precise (1); the file size increases because each sample takes more bits (1).
**Calculate (2 to 4 marks):** show formula, substitution, bits to bytes (/8) and units. Method marks are given even if the arithmetic is wrong, so show every step.
**Convert units first:** minutes to seconds, kHz to Hz; examiners deliberately put values in awkward units.

**Discuss/evaluate (6 marks):** give points for both sides (quality vs size), use the correct technical words, link to the situation given in the question (e.g. streaming over a slow connection), and finish with a justified conclusion.
**Trade-off wording:** 'higher quality, but larger file size, so more storage space and bandwidth are needed' is a safe high-mark phrase.
**Graph tips:** describe the trend (straight line through origin = directly proportional), quote values from the axes with units and read carefully from the scale.
**Keep the three ideas separate:** sample rate (how often), bit depth (how precisely), duration (how long). Naming the right one in each sentence earns the technical-term mark.

mistakes.r: A higher sample rate takes more samples per second, giving a closer (more accurate) copy of the original sound. Loudness is amplitude and pitch is frequency.
mistakes.w: Saying a higher sample rate makes the sound louder or higher pitched.

mistakes.r: Sample rate is the number of samples per second (Hz); bit depth is the number of bits used for each sample.
mistakes.w: Mixing up sample rate and bit depth, e.g. 'bit depth is how many samples per second'.

mistakes.r: Convert to seconds (x 60) before multiplying; the formula needs the duration in seconds.
mistakes.w: Leaving the duration in minutes when calculating file size.

mistakes.r: The formula gives bits; divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for kB and 1,000,000 for MB, only as far as the question asks.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to divide by 8 to convert bits to bytes (or dividing by 8 when the answer is wanted in bits).

mistakes.r: Convert kHz to Hz by multiplying by 1,000 before using the formula.
mistakes.w: Using kHz as if it were Hz (e.g. using 44.1 instead of 44,100).

mistakes.r: Say the recording is closer to / a more accurate copy of the original sound because more samples are taken (or each sample is more precise).
Give both sides: higher quality but a larger file size (more storage and bandwidth); low settings give a smaller file but lower quality.
mistakes.w: Only giving the benefit of high settings.

mistakes.r: Sound is stored as binary numbers, one for each sample, and converted from analogue by an ADC.
mistakes.w: Writing that sound is stored as an analogue wave or 'sound waves' on the computer.

mistakes.r: Duration only changes the file size, not the quality.
mistakes.w: Thinking the longer recording sounds better.

summary: You must know that sound is analogue and is stored digitally by taking regular samples of its amplitude, and that the sample rate (Hz), the bit depth (bits per sample) and the duration (seconds) decide the quality and the size of a sound file. You must also be able to calculate file size = sample rate x bit depth x duration, and explain the quality versus file size trade-off.

terms.d: A continuous signal that can take any value within a range, such as a real sound wave.
Data represented as a limited set of separate values, stored by a computer as binary.
Measuring the amplitude of a sound wave at regular intervals of time so it can be stored digitally.
One measurement of the amplitude of the sound wave at one instant.
The number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The unit of frequency or sample rate: one cycle or one sample per second.
1,000 hertz; 44.1 kHz is 44,100 samples per second.
The number of bits used to store each sample; more bits allow more possible amplitude levels.
The length of a sound recording, measured in seconds.
The height of a sound wave, which determines how loud the sound is.
The number of wave cycles per second (Hz); it determines the pitch of a sound.
A device that converts an analogue signal into digital (binary) data by sampling it.
A device that converts digital data back into an analogue signal so it can be played through a speaker.
The amount of storage used by a file; for sound = sample rate x bit depth x duration (in bits).
Rounding each sampled amplitude to the nearest value that can be stored using the available bit depth.
Reducing the size of a file; lossy removes some data permanently, lossless keeps all the original data.

worked.q: A music track is recorded with a sample rate of 44,100 Hz and a bit depth of 16 bits. The track lasts 3 minutes. Calculate the file size in megabytes. Assume one channel and no compression. [4 marks]
steps: File size (bits) = sample rate x bit depth x duration = 44,100 x 16 x 180.

worked.q: A sound recording lasts 5 seconds and has a bit depth of 16 bits. Its file size is 400,000 bytes. Calculate the sample rate used. [3 marks]
steps: Sample rate = file size / (bit depth x duration) = 3,200,000 / (16 x 5).
Check: 40,000 x 16 x 5 = 3,200,000 bits = 400,000 bytes, which matches.

worked.ans: Model answer: Taking fewer samples per second (low sample rate) and storing each sample with fewer bits (low bit depth) means the recording is less accurate and further from the original sound, so the quality is lower. However, there is less data, so the file size is smaller and takes less storage space and bandwidth.
worked.q: A student records a voice message using a low sample rate and a low bit depth. Explain the effect on the quality and the file size of the recording. [4 marks]
steps: Point 1: a low sample rate means fewer samples are taken per second.
Point 2: so the digital recording is a less accurate copy of the original sound and detail is lost.
Point 3: a low bit depth means fewer bits are used to store each sample, so fewer amplitude levels are available and each value is less precise.
Point 4: because there are fewer samples and each uses fewer bits, the file size is smaller (less storage and quicker to send).
